opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the reason it's so direct is that, at the level of mathematics, the two problems are essentially the same kind of problem. When you jam particles, say grains of sand or soft spheres in a box, you can describe the system by an energy that is zero when no particles overlap and positive when they do. So you have a set of constraints, one for each pair of particles in contact, and the question is whether you can satisfy all of them at once. If you have few particles in a big volume, it's easy: there's a whole landscape of zero-energy configurations, and the system is floppy, it flows. As you increase the density, at some point you can no longer satisfy all the constraints, and the system becomes rigid. That's the jamming transition.

Now look at a neural network trained on a classification task with a hinge-type loss. Each training example that is not fitted correctly with some margin contributes a positive term to the loss, and each correctly fitted example contributes nothing. So again you have a set of constraints, one per data point, and the degrees of freedom are the weights instead of particle positions. If you have many parameters relative to the number of data points, you can satisfy all the constraints, the loss goes to zero, and you find yourself in a big, flat, connected region of solutions. If you have too few parameters, you can't, and you're stuck at positive loss. In between there is a sharp transition, and it turns out to be in the same universality class, or at least to share many of the same properties, as jamming.

What makes it more than a loose metaphor is that the quantitative predictions carry over. In jamming there is a counting argument, essentially Maxwell's argument for rigidity: at the transition, the number of constraints, the contacts, equals the number of degrees of freedom. We found the same thing in networks: at the transition, the number of data points that are unsatisfied, that sit at the margin, is of the order of the number of parameters. And you see the same signatures in the spectrum of the Hessian: lots of near-zero modes, a characteristic singular behavior near the transition, which in packings shows up in the density of vibrational modes.

And then there's a practical lesson. In the jammed phase, the landscape is glassy and rough, and gradient descent gets stuck. But just above the transition, in the overparametrized phase, the landscape becomes surprisingly benign: you don't get trapped in bad minima because there are so many flat directions. That gives you a physical way to understand why overparametrization helps optimization. It also connects to the double-descent phenomenon: the peak in test error happens precisely at this jamming point, because there the solution is extremely sensitive, the norm of the network output fluctuates wildly with the initialization, a bit like how a marginally jammed packing responds very strongly to small perturbations.

So for me it's direct because it's not just that both are "rugged landscapes" in some vague sense. It's that both are constraint-satisfaction problems with continuous degrees of freedom and a cost function that vanishes when constraints are satisfied, and that structure alone dictates a lot of the geometry, the critical behavior, and even some of the generalization properties.

r001.rationale: It describes particles constrained not to overlap and network weights constrained to fit each data point, explicitly treating both as constraint-satisfaction problems.

r002.rationale: It says both problems have continuous degrees of freedom and describes the network transition as in the same universality class as jamming.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's direct because, at the end of the day, it is the same mathematical problem. When you take grains of sand, or any hard particles, and you compress them, at some point they stop being able to flow. They jam. And the reason they jam is that the number of constraints, the contacts between particles that cannot overlap, becomes equal to the number of degrees of freedom you have to move them around. This is the Maxwell counting argument, essentially: you count how many things you want to satisfy and how many ways you have to satisfy them, and at the jamming point they balance exactly. That is what gives jamming its very peculiar properties: marginal stability, soft modes, a diverging number of nearly unstable directions.

Now look at a classifier. You have a network with some number of parameters, and you have a training set of, say, N examples, and for each example you want the margin, the output, to be on the right side of some threshold. If you use a hinge loss, each example is exactly a constraint of the type "this quantity must be larger than that one," which is the same mathematical structure as "these two particles must not overlap." A satisfied example contributes zero loss, just like two particles that don't touch contribute zero energy. An unsatisfied one costs something that grows with how far you've violated the constraint.

So when you train, you are literally trying to find a configuration of the parameters where all the constraints are satisfied. If the network is large compared to the dataset, it's easy: you have many more degrees of freedom than constraints, you find a solution with zero loss, and the landscape there looks flat. That is the "unjammed" phase. If the network is small, you cannot satisfy everything, and you end up stuck in a glassy landscape with many unsatisfied constraints, which is the jammed phase. And the interesting thing is that the transition in between is sharp, and it is controlled by exactly the same counting: the number of examples that remain "active," sitting right at the margin, becomes comparable to the number of parameters.

What really convinced me that it was not just a loose metaphor is that the predictions are quantitative. The critical exponents, the way the number of unsatisfied constraints scales as you approach the transition, the structure of the Hessian with its flat directions, we could compute these from the jamming theory and then check them in actual networks, and they matched. The spectrum of the Hessian near the transition shows this abundance of low-frequency modes that we know very well from jammed packings. So it is not that the loss landscape "resembles" a sandpile in some poetic way. It is that the same constraint-satisfaction geometry produces the same singular behavior, and you can transfer the tools, and the intuition, from one field to the other almost without modification.

r001.rationale: The response directly compares particles constrained not to overlap with model parameters constrained to satisfy each training example.

r002.rationale: It says the systems share constraint-satisfaction geometry and singular behavior, but does not clearly state that continuously variable constraint-satisfaction problems belong to a common universality class.

astra-6.text:
Well, in both cases you can think of the problem as satisfying a large number of constraints. For particles, the constraints are simply that they should not overlap. For a neural network, they are that the outputs should agree with the training labels.

You can make the analogy very concrete by considering soft particles: whenever two particles overlap, you assign an energy cost. The total energy is then a sum of penalties for violated constraints, just like a training loss. If you have enough freedom, you can find a configuration where all the constraints are satisfied and the energy is zero. If there are too many constraints, you cannot. Jamming is the boundary between these two regimes.

In learning, the corresponding transition is the point where the model becomes expressive enough to fit the training set. The particle coordinates are replaced by the parameters of the model, but you are still asking about the geometry of a space of variables subject to constraints.

What makes this useful is that the analogy goes beyond saying that both landscapes are complicated. You can ask how many constraints become binding at the transition, which directions remain soft, and how the curvature behaves. Those are precise questions in both systems. Of course, the constraints in a neural network have a different structure, so the analogy does not imply that every property is identical.

r001.rationale: It pairs particle non-overlap constraints with fitting training labels using model parameters.

r002.rationale: It discusses shared constraint geometry but does not state that such problems belong to a common universality class.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, in both cases you have a large number of variables that must satisfy a large number of constraints. For particles, the variables are their positions, and the constraints are that they cannot overlap. In a learning problem, the variables are the weights, and each training example imposes a constraint on the output.

You can make this correspondence quite explicit. For soft particles, you assign an energy cost to overlaps. In learning, you assign a loss to violated constraints. Then you ask whether you can find a configuration with zero energy, or zero training loss. Jamming is the boundary where satisfying all the constraints becomes impossible.

The perceptron is a particularly clean example: depending on its parameters, its constraint landscape can have the same critical properties as particle jamming. So the analogy is not simply that both landscapes are complicated. In certain models, you can use the same mathematical description to understand the transition and the marginal stability near it. For deep networks, the correspondence is less exact, but it gives us a useful starting point.

r001.rationale: It directly maps particle positions constrained to avoid overlap to model weights constrained by training examples.

r002.rationale: It says a perceptron can share jamming’s critical properties, but does not state that constraint-satisfaction problems with continuously variable degrees of freedom belong to a common universality class.
